investigations.title: Arctic, coast and Plains: work, knowledge and belonging
investigations.question: How do different communities sustain life and pass on knowledge?
investigations.orientation: Inspect a carved tool, wooden-household evidence, a hunting landscape, gardens, clothing and a primary title page. Six distinct contexts show how practical work, shared responsibilities and interpretation matter. Similar needs never make these peoples interchangeable.
investigations.geography: Selected places in the Bering Strait, Canadian Arctic, Olympic Peninsula, southern Alberta, Missouri valley and northern Vancouver Island. The inquiry crosses centuries; its sequence is not a documented route or claim of contact.
investigations.limits: Two selected contexts for each of three broad regions. Many Inuit homelands, Thule/Dorset histories, Northwest Coast nations and Plains communities still need fuller treatment. Later photographs, reconstructions, disputed dates and community sources remain explicit.

Documents and places record particular histories, not one universal woodland way of life.

investigations.limits: Selected northeastern, Great Lakes and southeastern histories, with earlier Hopewell context. Many nations and earlier chronological windows still need fuller treatment. journeys.title: Independence, citizenship and the work after a promise
journeys.question: What changes on a political turning point—and what still has to be built?
journeys.introduction: Follow four investigations in chronological order. They are comparisons of political change, not a claim that one caused the next. Read a proclamation, a border timetable, a stamp and a voting photograph; ask who gained power, who could participate and what remained unsettled.

stops.subject: indonesia-independence
stops.title: A proclamation begins a struggle
stops.narrative: Inspect the signatures and the short text. Use the phases to distinguish the declaration from Dutch recognition and the later unitary state.

stops.subject: partition-1947
stops.title: A political date and a disrupted home
stops.narrative: Follow the independence and boundary-announcement sequence. Use the place study to ask why a national milestone did not settle every family’s security.

stops.subject: ghana-independence
stops.title: New words on an older design
stops.narrative: Find what changed on the stamp and what remained underneath. Then read the debate to identify the powers that changed hands at independence.

stops.subject: south-africa-rights
stops.title: Bind a government to rights
stops.narrative: Move from the 1994 voting photograph to the 1996 constitutional text. Distinguish the right to govern from the rights that constrain government.

journeys.conclusion: A proclamation, a transfer of sovereignty, an election and a constitutional right do different work. Each can change institutions without settling every question of safety, participation or material life. Explain the particular mechanism before comparing outcomes.

evidence.prompt: Which conclusion best uses the evidence encountered on this journey?

options.text: A national independence date establishes when everyone gained equal rights and secure livelihoods.
options.feedback: The documents identify political changes. They do not measure every person’s rights, safety or livelihood.

options.text: Different milestones change different powers; later outcomes need evidence beyond the announcement or image.
options.feedback: The proclamation, stamp, border timetable and constitution let you identify specific changes and ask a separate question about their effects.

options.text: Because these transitions involved institutions, ordinary people played no part in them.
options.feedback: The Ghana account describes organizing networks, and the South African sources discuss public participation. Institutional history also involves people’s work.

journeys.title: Skills, records and protection
journeys.question: How can we distinguish skilled work from effective protection?
journeys.introduction: Compare a reported factory investigation, a published mill depiction and a reform photograph with their separately dated records. Each setting had its own workers, institutions and legal scope. These stops organize questions, not a route, a shared workforce or a single causal story from machines or images to protection.

stops.subject: factory-reform
stops.title: Separate an investigative action from a completed result
stops.narrative: The 1833 Act’s selected clauses define powers and covered categories. The 1836 extract reports an inspector questioning boys, examining a time book and intending punishment. Ask what the selected record establishes and what would require evidence of what happened afterward. The extract does not supply every age, break, book finding or completed penalty, and a reported benefit elsewhere is not a census of all workplaces.

stops.subject: tomioka
stops.title: Connect the pictured workplace with learned skills
stops.narrative: Observe the print’s rows of people, equipment and roof supports as an artistic arrangement. Its NDL catalogue attribution is bracketed [1872]; the modern reproduction has another, unknown date. Separate sources explain women learning filament handling and teaching elsewhere, alongside regional farming, schooling and later cold storage. Neither the orderly picture nor technical learning establishes everyone’s working conditions. The 1911 law and its 1916 implementation are later, separate evidence.

stops.subject: hine-labor
stops.title: Keep photograph, caption and later administration distinct
stops.narrative: The case remains the particular photograph and caption dated 3 December 1908. Looking supports observations; the caption supplies Hine’s disputed workplace account. A later federal law and the Bureau’s report concern different dates and a defined administrative scope. They do not identify this child’s age, prove every mill complied or establish that this single photograph caused legislation. Ask which further record could test a particular claim.

journeys.conclusion: Explain a practical task with a particular source, then name the evidence needed to assess a worker’s protection. Training, an artistic arrangement, an investigative action and a legal rule answer related questions without becoming the same kind of proof. Preserve the people, places, dates and access limits of each record.

evidence.prompt: Which conclusion distinguishes the supplied records carefully?

options.text: A source may explain a skill or report an investigation without proving effective protection for everyone.
options.feedback: The records have defined purposes and scopes. Evidence of training or an investigative action is not automatically a complete account of working conditions or outcomes.

options.text: Orderly rows in the Tomioka print prove that every worker could rest or leave whenever she wished.
options.feedback: A published artistic arrangement does not establish every worker’s hours or freedom. Those questions require appropriate records and attributed accounts.

options.text: The Hine photograph alone proves that it caused a later law and that every factory complied.
options.feedback: The photograph, caption, law and administration report have separate dates and evidentiary roles. A single image cannot supply that causal or universal outcome claim.

interval.label: 1945–1950 · a selected transition and aftermath
interval.note: A teaching window, not the lifespan of India or Pakistan and not an end date for displacement or memory.

phases.title: A later departure in Bengal

contexts.title: Textile work, schooling and inspection: selected 1833–1836 records

interval.label: Selected statute and enforcement evidence, 1833–1836
interval.note: This reference is an evidence sequence around the unchanged case, not industrialization’s lifespan or a claim that all factories changed together. The Act’s passage and commencement provisions are different dates. Quarry Bank provides broader background; the Science Museum’s catalogued 1927 machine is later and is not placed within these phases.

contexts.summary: A rule needed people, records and institutions to operate. These selected sources distinguish covered work, statutory obligations, an inspector’s investigation and contested evidence of results.

citations.locator: Lesson PDF, printed p. 9, Source 1 transcript

phases.label: 1833: the Act is passed
phases.title: 29 August dates a statute, not completed workplace change
phases.text: The Act names powered textile processes and regulates children and young persons through restrictions, schooling, certification and inspection. Its exceptions and commencement provisions matter. Its title does not turn it into a ban on all child work or a complete protection for every worker.

citations.locator: PDF 1: title/date and clause I; selected provisions

phases.label: 1834: selected provisions begin; others are phased
phases.title: The date of passage differs from implementation dates
phases.text: Clauses I and VII specify 1 January 1834 for their restrictions; clause VIII phases further age coverage over later months and contains a silk proviso. These are statutory instructions, not a measured series of compliance. The draft does not replace their detail with one universal daily-hours number.

citations.locator: PDF 1, clause I; PDF 3, clauses VII–VIII

phases.label: 1836: Parliament debates enforcement and alteration
phases.title: Reports become evidence in a contested political decision
phases.text: On 9 May, speakers disputed the law’s operation and a proposed change. Hindley quoted Inspector Howell describing instances of benefit, especially reduced night work; other speakers raised household earnings and practical difficulties. A parliamentary argument is not a neutral national compliance survey.

phases.label: 1836: an inspector describes a particular investigation
phases.title: A reported complaint requires evidence about what followed
phases.text: The institution dates the Taylor, Ibbotson & Co. extract to 1836. The inspector reports questioning boys, looking at a time book and intending punishment. The selected transcription does not provide ages, every break, the book’s findings or a completed penalty; it cannot alone measure all workplaces.

contexts.title: Silk work: learning, adaptation and the limits of protection

interval.label: Selected mill, training, storage and legal changes, 1872–1916
interval.note: A selected source frame from Tomioka’s opening to Factory Act implementation, extending four years beyond the Meiji period. It is not the mill’s operating lifespan or the beginning/end of Japanese industrialization. The earlier 1863 farmhouse and a later 1917 worker recollection are explicitly contextual comparisons. The original exact October 1872 case remains unchanged. Memoir writing/publication, modern scholarship, heritage listing and digitization have separate dates.

contexts.summary: Imported machinery depended on trained hands, local materials and people raising silkworms. Learning and technical change could coexist with restrictive working arrangements and incomplete legal protection.

phases.label: October 1872: the model mill opens
phases.title: A new mill uses established regional skills
phases.text: French machinery and advice met Japanese building work and an existing sericultural region. Opening the mill did not create the whole production system in one year or determine every employee’s later experience.

phases.label: 1874: trained workers teach at another mill
phases.title: Learning can travel through people
phases.text: The NDL places Wada Ei(ko)’s departure from Tomioka in July 1874 and subsequent teaching at Saijō, later Rokkōsha. Nakamura and Molteni discuss material changes at that separate Matsushiro mill through her later recollection. This is not an account freshly written during the visit or a reconstruction of Tomioka’s equipment.

phases.label: 1884: Takayama-sha becomes a school
phases.title: Controlling a living crop requires practice
phases.text: Students learned sericulture through practical rearing. Ventilation, warmth and humidity mattered to silkworms before cocoons reached a reel. The school’s date is distinct from the mill’s opening and from Tajima’s earlier 1863 farmhouse.

phases.label: 1905: Arafune’s first storage units operate
phases.title: Storage changes the timing of work
phases.text: Keeping eggs cool delayed hatching. Labels and catalogues helped staff return egg cards when needed. These early twentieth-century facilities did not exist at the mill’s 1872 opening, and their later functional association is not a mapped shipment itinerary.

phases.label: 28 March 1911: Factory Act promulgation
phases.title: Making a law and applying it have different dates
phases.text: The National Archives distinguishes the 1911 law from its later implementation. Protective provisions had a defined initial scope, rather than instantly covering every person working with silk.

phases.label: September 1916: implementation begins
phases.title: Protection needs evidence of how it works
phases.text: The law came into force after a five-year delay. Nakamura and Molteni describe exceptions affecting silk-reeling and evidence of continuing long hours in Nagano. This is a qualified regional comparison, not a finding that every Tomioka shift violated or complied with the law.

contexts.title: Photographic investigation, child-labor rules and enforcement in the United States

interval.label: Selected campaign and federal-administration frame, 1904–1918 CE
interval.note: An orientation frame from the NCLC’s founding through a particular federal act’s operation and constitutional reversal. It preserves the selected case’s complete 3 December 1908 interval. The 1921 report publication and 2019 institutional interpretation are later evidence clocks, not extensions of this frame. This is neither the beginning of all US labor organizing nor the end of child labor.

contexts.summary: Investigators made working conditions visible through photographs, captions, reports and exhibits. Enforcing age and hour rules required different work: checking evidence, issuing certificates and inspecting workplaces. A campaign, a statute and its administration answer different questions.

citations.locator: Background and Scope; The Photo Captions

phases.label: 1904: the institutional founding date
phases.title: An organization assembles a reform campaign
phases.text: The Library of Congress dates the NCLC’s founding to 1904. Its collection account describes investigation and publicity aimed at working children’s conditions. Founding one organization is not the origin of every labor campaign or proof that all families shared its program.

phases.label: 3 December 1908: the catalogued photograph date
phases.title: A particular mill scene enters a documented series
phases.text: The selected catalogue caption places the spinner at Mollahan Mills, Newberry, and reports the overseer’s denial. A separate group caption from that mill is also dated 3 December 1908. Related records allow comparison without making either picture a census, a verified age record or the same view.

citations.locator: Existing photo; indexed caption title, Hine 358 / nclc.01451

phases.label: 1913: a change in Hine’s NCLC role
phases.title: Photographs circulate through exhibits as well as print
phases.text: The collection account dates Hine’s promotion to head of the exhibits department to 1913. It describes photographs circulating in reports, publications, slide shows and displays. These uses explain intended audiences and publicity work; they do not measure each viewer’s response.

citations.locator: Background and Scope: distribution and exhibits

phases.label: 1 September 1916: approval of a particular act
phases.title: Congress links product shipment to age and hour conditions
phases.text: The Keating-Owen Act restricted interstate or foreign shipment of specified products made under prohibited child-employment conditions. It authorized inspections and provided for certificates. Its enactment was a legal step with a defined reach, not a direct result established for this single photograph or proof of compliance.

phases.label: 1 September 1917: the act takes effect
phases.title: Age evidence becomes an administrative task
phases.text: The Children’s Bureau report identifies this effective date. Its certificate discussion explains why trustworthy age evidence and coordination with state systems mattered. The report distinguishes those administrative arrangements from simply printing an age rule.

phases.label: Spring 1918 inspections; 3 June constitutional decision
phases.title: Inspection findings and a court ruling change the inquiry
phases.text: The report records underage employment and certificate gaps in a defined South Carolina inspection sample before the act was declared unconstitutional on 3 June. It also records later investigations under other authority and longer hours at the South Carolina factories revisited. This is a particular observed sequence, not proof that every protection or inspection ceased.

contexts.title: Kwakwaka’wakw witnesses, prohibition and particular returns

interval.label: Selected law, community institution and return records, 1884–2003
interval.note: The complete original 1884–1980 case remains unchanged. Later returns in this reference do not move its endpoint, establish that every belonging returned or date the origins of potlatch. The 1884 amendment and 1885 commencement are distinct; 1980 opening and a particular 2003 return are separate events.

contexts.summary: Witnesses, family work and care for belongings give potlatch its consequences in the public explanations selected here. Prohibition, confiscation and return changed circumstances without making government or museum custody the sole authority over community knowledge.

citations.locator: Start and End of the Potlatch Ban

phases.label: 1884: amendment in U’mista’s history
phases.title: A law targets an institution
phases.text: U’mista dates the amendment to 1884. This is a government action against an existing practice, not the beginning of potlatch or evidence that people stopped participating.

phases.label: 1885: law takes effect in Living Tradition’s account
phases.title: Commencement is a different date
phases.text: Living Tradition gives 1 January 1885 for the prohibition taking effect. The two dates answer different questions about the legislation.

citations.locator: The Start of the Potlatch Ban

phases.label: 1921: Dan Cranmer’s Village Island potlatch
phases.title: A particular gathering and later prosecution
phases.text: The community history places Dan Cranmer’s potlatch at Village Island and describes prosecutions and confiscation afterward. The title page published in the same year is a different document, not a record of that gathering.

phases.label: 1922: surrender and detention in the community accounts
phases.title: Belongings were taken under pressure
phases.text: The public accounts connect coerced surrender of belongings with sentences after the potlatch. Vera Newman and Chief Bill Cranmer describe particular family experiences and the pressure exerted. Their statements do not become an identical experience for every family.

citations.locator: Impact transcript and named speaker captions

phases.label: 1951: prohibition removed
phases.title: A legal change does not instantly repair harm
phases.text: Living Tradition dates the removal to 1951; Barb Cranmer describes the continuing fear and the time needed to feel secure participating openly. The legal milestone and family confidence are different changes.

citations.locator: The End of the Potlatch Ban

phases.label: 1974: U’mista Cultural Society formed
phases.title: Return requires organized negotiation
phases.text: The Society’s history dates its formation to 22 March 1974. The return account describes families and communities planning institutions to house belongings; this is not proof that all return negotiations were already completed.

phases.label: 1980: U’mista opens
phases.title: A home for care, language and history
phases.text: U’mista opened in November 1980. The public return page identifies family members with returned belongings at that opening, while the wider account describes decisions about where family treasures would be held.

phases.label: 2003: a particular headdress return in the source caption
phases.title: Return histories continue beyond the case
phases.text: The public caption records Chief William T. Cranmer with Aube Elléouët on 23 September 2003 and says she returned a headdress surrendered by Chief Sam Scow in 1922. This is one documented return account, not a complete chain of custody or the end of repatriation.

citations.locator: Chief William T. Cranmer and Aube Elléouët, 23 September 2003

contexts.title: Printed government, coercion and renewed publication

interval.label: Selected constitution-to-renewed-newspaper frame, 1827–1844 CE
interval.note: A selected sequence from the 1827 constitution through the Advocate’s 1844 establishment in Tahlequah. The whole original 1821–1839 inquiry remains unchanged. Neither end dates Cherokee nationhood, language, printing or the end of enslavement. The 1828 April photograph, February first-issue transcription and 1832 reprints retain separate issue dates.

contexts.summary: Print carried laws, practical staffing concerns and disagreement to readers. Forced removal disrupted lives and government without ending publication or nationhood; the renewal of institutions did not create equal rights for everyone.

citations.locator: Publication heading and July 1827 adoption; Article III
Conflicts with Georgia; Forced Removal and Reunification, including1844 Advocate
Slavery in Cherokee Nation;1839 timeline entry

phases.label: July 1827: a written constitution
phases.title: National authority includes political exclusions
phases.text: The later first-issue transcription identifies a constitution formed at New Echota in July 1827. It describes national land and divided government while restricting office and voting by sex, freedom and ancestry.

citations.locator: Adoption heading; ArticlesI–III, especiallyIII sections 4 and 7

phases.label: 1828: separate newspaper issues
phases.title: Preserve publication and object identities
phases.text: The February 21 first-issue transcription carries the constitution. The unchanged supplied photograph identifies the April 10 title portion, vol. 1 no. 8; it is not the February first issue and has an unknown later photographic-reproduction date.

citations.locator: Retained catalogue scope; actual unchanged masthead

phases.label: September/October 1832: staffing and publication are debated
phases.title: The newspaper contains different speakers
phases.text: Boudinot’s dated letter discusses assistance and a vacancy. A separate correspondent debates how to seek Ross’s views, while an October reprint urges continued publication. These pieces are distinct from a single uncontested editorial voice.

citations.locator: September 15 issue: letter and separate September 7 reply
October 6 issue: Christian Soldier attribution and comment

phases.label: 1835: contested treaty authority
phases.title: Signatures are not universal consent
phases.text: The Cherokee Nation’s historical account states that New Echota signatories lacked authority under Nation law. The account distinguishes their act from the position of the majority who opposed relinquishing their homelands.

citations.locator: Conflicts with the State of Georgia

phases.label: 1838–1839: forced removal
phases.title: Political pressure becomes coercive movement
phases.text: The Nation’s account describes U.S. troops enforcing removal. Its public Freedmen history includes people enslaved by Cherokee citizens in this forced movement. No single route or uniform legal position is inferred for everyone.

citations.locator: Forced Removal, Internal Conflict, and Reunification

phases.label: 1839: reorganization without universal equality
phases.title: Political continuity includes continuing conflict
phases.text: A new constitution reorganized the Nation after removal and earlier western migration. The public Freedmen history records continuing racial inequality. The date does not mark the end of internal conflict or slavery.

citations.locator: Reunification under a new constitution; persistent disputes

phases.label: 1844: the Cherokee Advocate is established
phases.title: Publication resumes in a changed setting
phases.text: The Cherokee Nation’s account identifies the bilingual Advocate in Tahlequah alongside rebuilt institutions. It is evidence of continued publication, not proof that removal’s consequences or political exclusions were resolved.

contexts.title: Manoomin work, selected treaty evidence and intertribal care

interval.label: Selected U.S. treaty, separate photograph and stewardship frame, 1837–1984 CE
interval.note: The bounds connect an 1837 U.S. treaty and the 1984 creation of GLIFWC; they do not date manoomin’s origins or all Ojibwe history. The whole original bracketed [1913] photographic case remains unchanged. Its probable Ontario setting is separate from the U.S. ceded territories; neither treaty jurisdiction nor a legal identity is assigned to the unnamed person. Later public accounts/brochure have their own dates and scopes.

contexts.summary: Gathering, finishing and caring for rice waters involve knowledge and repeated work. A treaty clause, an archival photograph and an intertribal institution document different aspects of that history without making every Great Lakes community one legal or political setting.

citations.locator: Actual catalogue: bracketed date and probable Ontario location
Opening1984 institutional account and reserved rights

phases.label: 29 July 1837: a particular treaty names gathering wild rice
phases.title: Retained rights concern specified places and parties
phases.text: Article 5 addresses hunting, fishing and gathering wild rice within the ceded territory. GLIFWC explains that the Ojibwe retained rights rather than receiving the origin of those rights from the United States. The text does not identify the later photograph’s setting or prove every implementation.

citations.locator: Article 5; Article 6 and dated close, printed p.492

phases.label: Catalogued [1913]: a separately situated photograph
phases.title: One archival scene leaves questions open
phases.text: LOC assigns the bracketed date and a probable Ontario location. The person is unnamed and the exact lake unknown. The picture does not transfer the U.S. treaty’s geography or legal framework to this person.

phases.label: 1984: GLIFWC is created
phases.title: An institution supports continuing tribal responsibilities
phases.text: GLIFWC’s account dates its creation to 1984 and describes resource assessments and stewardship supporting member tribes. The brochure also identifies rice-bed protection and enhancement from that year. This dates an institution, not the beginning of Indigenous knowledge or care.

contexts.title: Inuinnait clothing: seasonal work, new supplies and teaching

interval.label: Selected represented periods and community research, 1880s–2019
interval.note: A bounded frame following selected community-directed exhibit periods and the separately dated 2017–19 research workshops, not the beginning/end of Inuinnait clothing or people. The original case remains the Southern Party window 1913–16. The photograph’s exact exposure is unknown and its 1922 publication date remains separate. Reconstructed garments were made in modern workshops rather than in the periods they represent.

contexts.summary: Preparing skins, choosing supplies and teaching patterns made clothing an ongoing practical task. The community exhibit explains material changes alongside outside pressures and continued making by Inuinnait.

phases.label: 1880s: a represented clothing and seasonal-work frame
phases.title: Land, harvest and making were connected
phases.text: The community exhibit links winter sea-ice sealing and summer caribou/fish harvests with the materials of clothing. Its selected 1880s account describes copper/bone needles, sinew thread and skins. The displayed parka was researched and made much later; 1880 is not its actual manufacture date.

phases.label: 1913–16 observations; photograph published in 1922
phases.title: An expedition record names two people
phases.text: The report’s Southern Party window frames the selected case. Plate I names Ikpakhuak and Higilak in dancing costume. Publication and fieldwork context do not independently establish the exposure’s exact date or location, and the photograph does not identify who sewed these particular garments.

citations.locator: Retained title-page scope; actual Plate I; archive metadata

phases.label: 1930s: the exhibit traces changes beginning in the 1920s
phases.title: Purchased materials entered clothing work
phases.text: The exhibit connects fox-fur exchange and trading posts with cotton covers, wool linings and steel tools. These selected changes concern access, work and choices; they do not mean every household adopted the same garment at one moment.

citations.locator: English body: exchange, materials and tools

phases.label: 1950s: settlement pressures and new supplies
phases.title: Making continued amid imposed changes
phases.text: PI/KHS describes government-directed changes in housing, work and schooling alongside continued hunting/fishing in outpost camps. Its clothing account includes ready-made supplies and hand-crank sewing machines. This attributed period account does not recover an identical experience for every family.

citations.locator: English body: government decisions and clothing

phases.label: 2017–19: researching, sewing and teaching
phases.title: Elders and learners made an exhibit for the future
phases.text: Mary Avalak, Mabel Etegik and Annie Atighioyak led the sewing program. Participants researched five historical parkas, prepared hides, made patterns and sewed modern reconstructions while documenting language and supporting new making for family and friends.

citations.locator: Creating Patterns of Change and Objects bodies

contexts.title: Te Tiriti: negotiation, asserted authority and early enforcement

interval.label: Selected negotiations and early colonial conflicts, 1840–1846
interval.note: A bounded frame from the first signings through the Northern War, not the Treaty’s lifespan, the whole colonization of Aotearoa or a common outcome for all iwi and hapū. The original exact 1840 case interval remains unchanged. Earlier He Whakaputanga, later land institutions, twentieth-century inquiries and a 2025 speech have separate dates. The close of this frame does not end Māori authority or continuing disputes.

contexts.summary: Making copies, interpreting words and gathering marks did not settle how authority would work. Crown proclamations and subsequent enforcement need evidence distinct from the signing record.

citations.locator: Northern War findings in official release

phases.label: 5–6 February 1840: discussion and the first signing
phases.title: An agreement is heard, debated and marked
phases.text: Rangatira heard the Māori text and verbal explanations at Waitangi before the first signatures on 6 February. Supporting and opposing speeches concerned authority, land and relations with newcomers. A later complete text does not preserve every spoken assurance.

citations.locator: Initial discussions; proposed Treaty; first signatures

phases.label: March–April 1840: different sheets and regional decisions
phases.title: One English sheet does not stand for every signing
phases.text: The Waikato-Manukau sheet is in English. Its first signing date is uncertain; an 11 April witness note is distinct from a 26 April Manukau signing. Some rangatira signed while Te Wherowhero declined. Neither choice describes every Waikato or Ngāti Whātua position.

phases.label: 21 May 1840: Hobson proclaims sovereignty
phases.title: The Crown announces a claim before circulation ends
phases.text: The proclamation asserts British sovereignty over the islands while sheets are still circulating. Ōnuku’s 30 May signing followed this announcement. A proclamation records what the Crown claimed; it does not establish every community’s consent or prove the promises were fulfilled.

phases.label: Early September 1840: the recorded signing process ends
phases.title: Absence and refusal remain part of the record
phases.text: The source records a final signing near Kāwhia on 3 September. The sheets did not reach every community, and some rangatira refused. The end of collecting marks was not an agreement on every interpretation or a referendum of all inhabitants.

phases.label: 1844–1846: disputes and the Northern War
phases.title: Enforcing authority changes people’s lives
phases.text: Hōne Heke and his followers challenged British authority by cutting the flagstaff at Kororāreka. Armed conflict followed. The Tribunal’s later Te Raki inquiry found serious Crown breaches in this period, including attacks on pā and kāinga and harm to non-combatants. These are district-specific historical findings, not a story of one uniform Māori response.

contexts.title: Satellite projects, observation and institutions: selected 1955–1958 records

interval.label: Selected satellite planning, launch and institutional responses, 1955–1958
interval.note: A bounded reference inquiry around an exact 1957 event, not the lifetime of Sputnik 1 or a complete 1945–1991 Cold War account. The registry’s broader institutional framework remains open. Later webpage editions, archive catalogues and anniversary exhibits are source-publication clocks, not ancient/event phases.

contexts.summary: An international scientific program gave satellite work a shared timetable while state priorities organized funding, secrecy and competition. A proposal, a completed launch and later arguments about observation or institutions establish different things.

phases.label: 1955: a public US satellite program for the IGY
phases.title: A common scientific timetable also became competitive
phases.text: NASA’s account dates the White House satellite announcement to July 1955 and the Vanguard selection to September. These are program decisions before the launch; the IGY itself ran from July 1957 through December 1958.

phases.label: January 1957: Korolev requests a simpler project
phases.title: A plan names organizations and a hoped-for date
phases.text: The 5 January proposal requests April–June launches, coordination across ministries and a radio/optical tracking system. The launch actually occurred in October. Proposed work and completed work must be checked against different records.

phases.label: October 1957: launch, announcement and observation
phases.title: One event entered several institutional arguments
phases.text: The 4 October launch is distinct from the Pravda announcement catalogued for 5 October and the 29 October Commons debate. The debate records both observation work and disagreement over national priorities, without standing for all British responses.

phases.label: 1958: new US institutions; IGY continues
phases.title: Institutional changes followed rather than defined the launch
phases.text: NASA’s timeline distinguishes the July Space Act, NASA opening in October and the IGY ending in December. These later decisions belong to the reference frame; the case retains its exact 1957 launch interval.

contexts.title: War decisions, correspondence, work and selected aftermath

interval.label: Selected decision, work and aftermath records,1914–1919
interval.note: The original whole 1914–1918 case is preserved.1919 belongs to selected retrospective administration and cemetery-care records, not a universal extension/end of fighting. The regional cases have their own intervals; source publication/transcription dates do not become wartime events.

contexts.summary: A European crisis involved contested government decisions, followed by mobilization through states and empires. Selected regional records make communication, civilian work, coercive recruitment and household consequences visible without making them one experience.

phases.label: 1914: decisions debated in public
phases.title: One government’s arguments are contested
phases.text: In the 3 AugustCommons discussion, Grey sets out the government’s position and MacDonald challenges the case for intervention. These are situated public arguments, not all diplomacy or a referendum of every population drawn into war.

phases.label: 1916: selected letters and factory records
phases.title: Mobilization reaches different kinds of work
phases.text: Named Indian correspondence and Birtley planning/factory records reveal different practical settings. Their shared war years do not establish a common journey, meeting or causal chain between the people described.

phases.label: 1917: recruitment and a separate public appeal
phases.title: Power and persuasion have different forms
phases.text: The selected South Nyeri research examines coercive recruitment. The existing USposter is a separate 1917 appeal to women. Neither source stands for the people or choices in the other setting.

phases.label: 1918: original major-war endpoint
phases.title: One timeline boundary does not settle every aftermath
phases.text: The conventional major-war interval remains 1914–1918. Regional fighting, movement and political consequences did not all begin or stop together; later care and administrative records have their own dates.

phases.label: 1919: selected work of recording and care
phases.title: Aftermath appears in particular documents
phases.text: Debauche’s care letter and Watkins’ retrospective report answer different questions after the selected wartime years. They cannot establish every household’s outcome or completion of all requested work.

contexts.title: Different war and persecution chronologies, 1931–1945

interval.label: Selected Asian and European war/persecution frame, 1931–1945
interval.note: A comparative orientation, not a new interval for world-war-two, one universal war start or a single policy imposed on all regions. The whole original 1933–1945 case remains intact.

contexts.summary: Japanese conquest, European warfare and the Holocaust have connected histories with different beginnings. Read regional institutions, people and records within their own dates.

citations.locator: German and Japanese Expansion; Invasion of Poland; Defeat of Germany; Defeat of Japan

phases.title: Japan invades Manchuria
phases.text: USHMM locates this conquest in September 1931; it precedes the later European war.

phases.title: The Holocaust’s persecution frame begins
phases.text: USHMM uses 1933–1945 for the evolving persecution and murder of European Jews. The original dossier keeps this frame.

phases.title: War expands in China
phases.text: The museum dates Japan’s invasion of China proper to July 1937.

phases.title: Germany invades Poland
phases.text: The museum places the start of World War II in Europe at Germany’s 1 September 1939 invasion.

phases.title: Different surrender dates
phases.text: Germany’s defeat in May and Japan’s formal surrender in September are distinct events within 1945.

citations.locator: Defeat of Germany; Defeat of Japan

comparisons.question: How can learning a production skill differ from putting worker protection into practice?
Which powers changed at independence, and what remained contested?
How does a change in government differ from a guarantee of political rights?
What is the difference between documenting work and changing its conditions?
How do factory systems organize skill and labor?
What separates an official document from people’s experience of political change?
What does a new political settlement promise, and what must be investigated afterward?
How do institutions and choices turn conflict into mass violence?
How does technical change depend on organized work?
How do material work and knowledge connect across generations?

orientations.title: Freedom, schooling and political participation
orientations.question: What changes when people win a declaration, a court case or an election?

summary.title: Saint-Domingue and Haiti
summary.text: In Saint-Domingue, people who had been enslaved fought to shape the meaning of emancipation. The French abolition decree of 1794 and Haitian independence in 1804 answered different questions: one concerned slavery, the other sovereignty. Neither date alone tells us how people could earn a living or exercise power afterward.

sections.title: Who could enter a classroom?
sections.text: In California, Mexican American families challenged segregation by local school districts. In Texas, Heman Sweatt challenged exclusion from a public law school. The courts addressed different institutions and questions. Reading the decisions side by side reveals how families and individuals tested public commitments in particular places.

citations.locator: Orange County family action and Ninth Circuit

sections.title: Political participation has a history beyond a single vote
sections.text: Mexico’s presidential election in 2000 brought an opposition candidate to office. The education ministry’s account distinguishes that transfer from the disagreements that followed. A change in office is something we can date; proving that it improved every citizen’s political voice would require further evidence.

citations.locator: Alternancia en el poder: election and subsequent disagreements

sections.title: A document can show one moment of work
sections.text: The linked Hine and Ojibwe readings ask who made a record and who supplied its interpretation. A reform photograph and later community knowledge can reveal tasks and relationships, but neither gives the unnamed subject’s complete testimony. The date of a photograph does not date the beginning of a practice.

citations.locator: Photograph LC-DIG-nclc-01451 and caption card no. 358

orientations.scope: Selected Caribbean, United States and Mexican settings. The legal examples are historical and differ in jurisdiction; no ruling or election is treated as continent-wide change.
orientations.perspectives: Formerly enslaved people, families bringing cases and voters appear as actors. Courts and governments record decisions more directly than the daily experience of everyone affected.

activity.prompt: Choose one victory in this reading. What did it change directly, and what would you need to know about its effects?
activity.response: Name the decision, year and jurisdiction. Then identify a different source—for example school enrolment, household testimony or later records—that could test implementation.

snapshots.text: In 1800, Saint-Domingue was still in the revolutionary struggle. The 1794 abolition decree preceded this moment; Haitian independence in 1804 had not yet been declared. Legal status, military control and the work of plantation communities cannot be reduced to a single date.

Around 1900, the 1896 Plessy decision remained a legal reference for enforced racial separation in the United States. Brown’s rejection of separate public schooling came in 1954. The intervening history must not be presented as though desegregation was already secured in 1900.

citations.locator: Historical introduction and opinion on Plessy

snapshots.text: In 1947 the Ninth Circuit upheld the ruling won by Mexican American families challenging segregation in Orange County schools. Mendez was a federal appeals decision, not the later US Supreme Court ruling in Brown and not a ruling integrating every school in the Americas.

In June 1950, the US Supreme Court ruled that Texas must admit Heman Sweatt to the University of Texas law school. It considered educational opportunities that could not be reduced to building size or a count of books. Brown’s broader public-school ruling was still four years away.

Mexico’s 2000 presidential election brought Vicente Fox, an opposition candidate, to office. This change after decades of rule by the dominant party is a specific political event. It does not establish that access to power or public services became equal for every citizen.

citations.locator: Election of Vicente Fox and limits of change

orientations.title: Asante and Benin courts, Gold Coast organizing and South African rights
orientations.question: What can an object, a political organization and a constitution each tell us about power?

summary.title: Skilled production and control
summary.text: At Kumasi, artisans made gold objects that expressed Asante court authority; gold also moved through tribute and war. Benin City was the centre of a different court. Britain’s 1897 attack and the later sale of looted works altered where objects could be seen and who could tell their histories.

citations.locator: Gold, tribute, artisans and court regulation

sections.title: Independence took organizing
sections.text: The United Gold Coast Convention formed in 1947. Nkrumah broke with it in 1949 and the Convention People’s Party launched its Positive Action campaign in 1950. An independence stamp of 1957 announced a later change, but the political work that preceded it included disagreement, strikes and repression.

citations.locator: Table A; Historical Setting: UGCC and Positive Action

sections.title: South Africa: voting and the limits of a promise
sections.text: The South African transition distinguished voting in 1994, constitutional signing in 1996 and commencement in 1997. The resulting text named rights and institutions; it did not measure whether every household could use those rights. A later national symbol similarly expresses an aspiration rather than proving an outcome.

orientations.scope: Asante/Gold Coast, Benin City and South Africa are distinct settings. The history of a particular museum acquisition is not the provenance of every Benin object.
orientations.perspectives: Court makers, organizers and voters broaden a story often told through rulers. Museum and government records still privilege particular institutions; a public emblem is not everyone’s testimony.

activity.prompt: How would you label a court object now in a museum if you know the general history of looting but not this object’s chain of custody?
activity.response: Give its supported production context, distinguish the documented attack from this object’s specific provenance, and say exactly which ownership steps remain unknown.

snapshots.text: Around 1800, Asante court production and gold exchange centred on institutions at Kumasi. The museum’s eighteenth–nineteenth-century weights and ornaments support this setting, without fixing their manufacture to 1800. These objects precede both the later Gold Coast colony and independent Ghana.

citations.locator: Court regulation and eighteenth–nineteenth-century object dates

snapshots.text: In 1900, British control was contested in Asante. In a separate setting, National Museums Scotland records purchases from a dealer during 1897–1903 following the British looting of Benin City. The two timelines concern different societies; the documented sales do not identify every object’s route.

In the Gold Coast in 1947, the United Gold Coast Convention formed. This was organization under colonial government, before the 1948 crisis, the later CPP split and 1957 independence. It supplies a specific African political setting without backdating the independence stamp.

In early 1950 the CPP’s Positive Action campaign called for strikes and resistance in the Gold Coast; leaders were imprisoned. The 1951 election and independence in 1957 came later. Political organizing did not mean that colonial executive power had already ended.

citations.locator: Historical Setting: Positive Action and 1951 election

snapshots.text: In April 2000 South Africa introduced a new coat of arms, after its first democratic election and the commencement of its final constitution. A new emblem marks a change in how the state presented itself; it cannot establish that unequal conditions had ended.

citations.locator: 2000: coat of arms on Freedom Day; constitutional milestones

orientations.title: Factory work, postwar recovery and institutions shared across borders
orientations.question: How can a proposal, an enacted rule and its effects have different dates?

summary.title: A mill needed rules and people to enforce them
summary.text: British cotton mills used apprentice labour around 1800. The 1802 legislation addressed apprentices; the 1833 Factory Act and its inspection system belong to a later stage. Surviving reports let us ask whether owners complied and what inspectors could actually see.

sections.title: After war, proposals became institutions in stages
sections.text: In 1947 George Marshall proposed American support for European recovery. The US law came in 1948. In 1950 Robert Schuman proposed sharing coal and steel production, especially between France and Germany. Reconstruction and political cooperation were related aims, but the speeches describe proposals, not instantaneous improvements in every home.

sections.title: A currency can change before the cash in a pocket
sections.text: The euro began in participating countries in 1999 for accounting and electronic payments. Euro notes and coins came in 2002. The distinction matters if a family story says what someone used to pay cash in 2000; a later coin cannot document that transaction.

orientations.scope: British industrial, French/German and selected participating European settings. These institutional changes did not encompass every European country or erase the uneven losses and displacement of war.
orientations.perspectives: Workers and households often appear indirectly in regulations, recovery proposals and monetary records. Their experiences require inspection reports, testimony and local evidence alongside the institutional dates.

activity.prompt: A museum label says a family paid cash with euro coins in France in 2000. How would you check it?
activity.response: Separate the 1999 currency launch from the 2002 issue of notes and coins. Ask whether the evidence describes accounting, electronic payment or physical cash, and identify the country.

snapshots.text: In Britain around 1800, apprentices worked in cotton mills before the 1802 apprentice legislation. The 1833 inspection system was still decades away. The later report in the factory dossier cannot be used as an inspector’s observation from 1800.

By 1900 Britain had already extended factory regulation beyond the earlier cotton-mill measures. Parliament’s 1867 extension is one dated step. A rule’s existence does not prove compliance in every workplace, and the earlier 1836 inspection material remains evidence from its own year.

On 5 June 1947 Marshall proposed a European plan for economic reconstruction with American assistance. Truman sent a related message to Congress in December. The legislation was signed in April 1948; a 1947 snapshot should show the proposal and need for recovery, not benefits already delivered under that Act.

citations.locator: 5 June speech, December message and 3 April 1948 Act

snapshots.text: On 9 May 1950 Schuman proposed placing French and German coal and steel production under common authority, open to other European participants. This is a dated proposal about resources, industry and war prevention, not evidence that every European state had already joined one organization.

citations.locator: Opening account and declaration: common High Authority

snapshots.text: In 2000 the euro existed for accounting and electronic payments in participating countries including France and Germany. National cash was still in use: euro banknotes and coins were introduced on 1 January 2002. Several European countries did not share the same currency timetable.

orientations.title: Qajar Iran, republican Türkiye and independent Kazakhstan
orientations.question: How can a photograph, a parliamentary record and a banknote establish different changes?

summary.title: Photographs at the Qajar court
summary.text: Qajar rulers governed Iran during the period conventionally dated 1785–1925. Photography arrived in the early 1840s and became one way the court presented itself and documented places. A staged image shows choices about representation; it cannot stand for all Iranian households.

citations.locator: Exhibition account: period, arrival of cameras and court missions

sections.title: The Ottoman imperial and republican settings differ
sections.text: After the First World War, an assembly met in Ankara in 1920 and proclaimed a republic in 1923. Parliamentary and electoral records describe formal changes in government. An American president’s 1947 request for assistance to Turkey and Greece reflects another government’s aims, not a survey of what Turkish citizens wanted.

citations.locator: New Parliament and Proclamation of the Republic

sections.title: In Central Asia, sovereignty also had practical forms
sections.text: Kazakhstan’s independence in 1991 and the introduction of the tenge in 1993 were separate steps. A banknote factory opened in 1995. Currency therefore offers a way to investigate the work of building institutions after Soviet rule, alongside the earlier Soviet space programme in the linked dossier.

orientations.scope: A Qajar court, selected Turkish institutions and Kazakhstan provide three local histories; neither an imperial label nor a modern border defines the whole region across two centuries.
orientations.perspectives: Court photographs, assemblies and a central bank speak from institutional positions. They document acts and objects more readily than regional differences, opposition voices or household purchasing power.

activity.prompt: Which would best date a political declaration, the creation of a currency and a family’s change in buying power?
activity.response: Use the declaration for the legal act and currency records for issue dates. Household income, prices and testimony would be needed for buying power; neither a new note nor a declaration alone establishes it.

snapshots.text: Around 1800 Iran was under Qajar rule, after the earlier Zand setting. The court photography discussed in this reading began only after cameras arrived in the 1840s. A Qajar photograph must not be backdated simply because the dynasty already existed.

In 1900 Qajar rule continued in Iran. The Berlin exhibition identifies a court photograph from 1893 and explains how photography helped construct images of rule. It supplies nearby dated evidence, not a picture taken in 1900 or an unfiltered view of all society.

In March 1947 Truman asked the US Congress for military and economic assistance to Greece and Turkey. Turkey’s republic had been proclaimed in 1923. The message records an American policy request, not money already received by every intended recipient or unanimous Turkish support.

Türkiye’s parliamentary election table records a general election on 14 May 1950. That entry establishes a dated electoral process; it does not by itself explain every voter’s choice or the extent of participation in each community. The selected Sputnik launch of 1957 still lay ahead.

By 2000 Kazakhstan had declared independence and introduced its own currency. The national bank dates those events to 1991 and 1993 respectively, and its banknote factory to 1995. These steps connect sovereignty with production without equating a change of currency with a guaranteed rise in living standards.

orientations.title: Company rule, Partition and the making of new political maps
orientations.question: When does changing a boundary also change the choices available to a household?

summary.title: Company territory was made through power
summary.text: Around 1800 the East India Company held territory under parliamentary oversight. Conquest and alliances expanded its holdings unevenly. In 1858 the British Crown took over the Company’s Indian possessions and armed forces; neither map nor administrative responsibility stayed fixed.

sections.title: A new border could divide a home from familiar places
sections.text: In 1947 independence and Partition divided Punjab and Bengal. A boundary map and official correspondence describe political decisions; later testimony can reveal uncertainty, displacement and loss that are harder to see on a map. Neither makes one household’s experience universal.

sections.title: New constitutions and internal boundaries came later
sections.text: India’s Constitution distinguished provisions effective immediately from general commencement in 1950. In 2000 Jharkhand became a state within India through the reorganization of Bihar. An internal state boundary and the 1947 international partition are different changes, even when both appear as lines on a map.

orientations.scope: Selected British Indian, Punjab/Bengal and post-independence Indian settings. The Indian commencement date is not a constitutional date for Pakistan or every South Asian state; internal reorganization is not another international partition.
orientations.perspectives: Official maps and laws are strong evidence of formal decisions. Compare them with personal records when asking about displacement, safety, language, work or the ability to return home.

activity.prompt: How would you distinguish a change of sovereign state from a change of state boundary within a country?
activity.response: Name the level of government and the legal event first. Then ask whose residence, citizenship or administration changed, using household-level evidence before making claims about lived effects.

snapshots.text: Around 1800, the East India Company expanded holdings through conquest and alliance under Governor-General Wellesley. This was Company government subject to parliamentary oversight, not yet the Crown takeover of 1858 and not a single uniform control over the whole subcontinent.

By 1900 the Crown had taken over the East India Company’s Indian possessions and armed forces under the 1858 Act. The earlier Company administration should not be left unchanged on a 1900 map. Nor should the 1947 border be projected backward into this period.

In August 1947 British India was partitioned as India and Pakistan became independent. Punjab and Bengal were divided. The decisions were dated; people’s journeys, losses and efforts to find relatives extended beyond the month in which sovereignty changed.

citations.locator: Independence and Partition background; selected telegrams

snapshots.text: 26 January 1950 was the general commencement date of India’s Constitution. Article 394 expressly distinguishes provisions that came into force at once. Independence in 1947 and constitutional commencement in 1950 belong to separate moments, not a shared date for all South Asian governments.

On 15 November 2000 Jharkhand became a state within India, formed from districts of Bihar. This was an internal reorganization rather than independence from India. The official formation date establishes the boundary change, not its effects on every resident.

orientations.title: From imperial and industrial settings to constitutions, war and talks
orientations.question: Which records tell us that an institution changed, and which describe its effects?

summary.title: China and Japan were not on one timetable
summary.text: The Qing court governed China across both the 1800 and 1900 snapshots. In Japan, Tomioka’s silk mill belonged to a nineteenth-century industrial project. Imported technology had to be adapted and workers had to learn new tasks; calling it modernization does not explain how work felt to each person.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: opening and integrated production

sections.title: Postwar Japan: commencement required further work
sections.text: Japan’s new constitution came into force in May 1947. Other laws were revised and a new Diet convened. A constitutional date matters, but it is not the same thing as the completion of every change in public institutions or family life.

citations.locator: Enactment and first session of the Diet

sections.title: Korea: a resolution and a declaration answer different questions
sections.text: The UN Security Council’s June 1950 resolution called for hostilities to cease and for North Korean forces to withdraw. Fifty years later, leaders met in Pyongyang and issued a joint declaration. A record of a demand or an agreement establishes what was asked or agreed, not that fighting instantly ended or political division vanished.

orientations.scope: Chinese imperial, Japanese industrial and constitutional, and Korean conflict/diplomatic settings. These national and international records do not describe a single East Asian political trajectory.
orientations.perspectives: Workers, families and those affected by war are unevenly visible in collections made by governments and international institutions. A leader’s statement does not establish every resident’s view.

activity.prompt: Which source could prove that leaders agreed to talks, and what would you need before claiming that families were reunited?
activity.response: Use the declaration for the commitment. Look for separately dated implementation records and family accounts before describing actual reunions or their reach.

snapshots.text: Around 1800 in China the Qing dynasty was in power. The National Library of Australia’s account places this in the longer 1644–1911 period. The selected Japanese mill at Tomioka is a later nineteenth-century setting; its machinery cannot be used to show industry in 1800.

Around 1900 Qing rule still continued in China, while Japan’s Tomioka mill had already opened in 1872. The two dates compare an imperial framework with an institution for silk production. The opening date does not establish which employee, machine or workplace rule applied in 1900.

Japan’s Constitution took effect on 3 May 1947, following April elections and before the first Diet session under it later in May. The National Diet Library lists further legal changes needed for the new institutions. Commencement therefore has a precise date without implying instantaneous implementation.

On 25 June 1950 the UN Security Council adopted resolution 82 in response to the armed attack on the Republic of Korea, calling for a halt to hostilities and withdrawal of North Korean forces. This records an institutional response to war, not a ceasefire already carried out.

citations.locator: Action note 25 June 1950; resolution title and operative demands

snapshots.text: In June 2000 the leaders of North and South Korea met in Pyongyang. Their joint declaration included commitments concerning separated families and cooperation. A summit and a written commitment are verifiable; the declaration alone does not prove reunification or that every family gained contact.

orientations.title: Aotearoa, Western Samoa and Indonesia: different paths through colonial rule
orientations.question: Why do contact, signing, recognition and independence need separate dates?

summary.title: Aotearoa before and after 1840
summary.text: Sealers and whalers arriving from the 1790s brought new maritime encounters to Māori communities before Te Tiriti was signed. In 1840 rangatira considered promises and signed or declined in particular circumstances. The several texts and later Crown actions must be distinguished from an assumption of universal agreement.

citations.locator: Sealers and whalers:1791–2 and early trade

sections.title: Indonesia: proclamation did not end the war
sections.text: The 1945 proclamation in Jakarta was followed by fighting and negotiations. Dutch military operations in 1947, the 1949 transfer to a federal state and the 1950 unitary change are separate events. They did not settle every territorial dispute or define one common civilian experience.

sections.title: Western Samoa had its own political movement
sections.text: Western Samoa passed from German to New Zealand administration. The Mau opposed colonial rule; New Zealand Parliament’s account describes the violent repression of a 1929 protest. The 1961 legislation and independence effective on 1 January 1962 belong to a different chronology from both Indonesia and Aotearoa.

citations.locator: Administration, Mau, Western Samoa Act and commencement

orientations.scope: Three selected settings. Western Samoa’s dates do not apply to American Samoa; Indonesian sovereignty and later East Timorese self-determination are separate processes. No general Pacific independence date is inferred.
orientations.perspectives: Treaty texts, colonial military accounts and legislatures document institutional acts. Rangatira, Samoan organizers and Indonesian civilians had distinct experiences that official records only partly preserve.

activity.prompt: Make a label for the 1950 Indonesian change and another for Western Samoa in 1962. Why should they use different verbs?
activity.response: In 1950 Indonesia replaced a federal arrangement with a unitary state following earlier proclamation and transfer. Western Samoa became independent in 1962. Name the prior status and authority each act changed.

snapshots.text: Around 1800 sealers and whalers were reaching Aotearoa waters; the ministry dates early arrivals to 1791–2 and describes links with the Australian port at Sydney. Te Tiriti’s 1840 signing was still in the future. Maritime contact is not a declaration of sovereignty.

By 1900 women in New Zealand had obtained the parliamentary vote under the 1893 Electoral Act, after petition campaigns. That change concerned voting rights; it did not resolve disagreements over Māori authority or mean that every political office became open at the same moment.

The Dutch launched a major military operation in Indonesia in July 1947, nearly two years after the independence proclamation. The 1949 federal settlement and 1950 unitary state were still in the future. A proclamation, control of territory and international recognition are different historical claims.

In 1950 Indonesia ended the federal structure created by the 1949 settlement and became a unitary state. Western Samoa remained under New Zealand administration; its independence would take effect in 1962. The two settings cannot share one decolonization date.

In 2000 East Timor was under the UN transitional administration established in 1999, following the popular consultation. Independent Timor-Leste dates to May 2002. The 2000 transition was neither the Indonesian revolution of 1945–50 nor independence already achieved.
